$comment: For government (/government/): what a government can do with or through The Labs. Unlisted draft (noindex), linked from the home page's footer. Written for the people who decide (workforce boards, economic development, agencies, library systems), a line at a time. The frame is work, wages, wealth in The Labs' own meaning: work in Arendt's sense (making something that lasts, as against labor that's used up), wages make it a job, wealth makes the labor of a job mean something. The model: free workshops (the competencies people need as work changes; digital and AI skills are one part), the open cycle anyone can join as a contributor at any time (with set windows for problem situations and proposals), and sector cohorts, by application, inside it. Sector cohorts are the main thing a government sponsors. Against RAISE US (see the project doc competition-raise-us.md), the page is the ground layer: where residents actually show up, radically open to contributions, curated by what works in practice, with delivery earned against a common standard (in design) and results published each cycle (placeholders until the fall numbers). 'Digital opportunity' is how the page speaks to digital-equity programs and funders. Don't use 'lighthouse sectors' (Governor Moore's term). The one action is a conversation, not the account: procurement staff don't make accounts. Research behind it: the project doc government-options-research.md.
title: For government
description: Free workshops and team projects where people learn by working on your region's real problems. Everything they make is open source, free for residents, communities, businesses, institutions and the city itself to use.

hero.title: Upskilling that adds up.
hero.lede: Free workshops and team projects where people learn by working on your region's real problems. Everything they make is open source, free for residents, communities, businesses, institutions and the city itself to use.
hero.alt: The Labs as a living network: an orb at the centre, with local Labs full of people and their projects orbiting it.

items.body: Making something that lasts and that others can use: a tool, a playbook, a better way to run a service. It outlives the hours that went into it.
What makes the labor of a job mean something. It keeps working for households and communities on its own.

where.title: In your communities, run by your residents.
where.lede: State programs and funds set the direction. The Labs is where people show up: free workshops and team projects close to home, run by volunteers who live there. It's the part of a workforce strategy residents can walk into this week.

items.label: Close to home
items.body: In public libraries and community spaces.

items.label: Run by residents
items.body: Volunteers who live there lead the workshops and keep the teams moving.

items.label: Open to anyone
items.body: Workshops are free, and there's nothing to apply for.

how.title: From a first workshop to a sector cohort.

items.title: Workshops
items.body: We're working out, in the open, which competencies people need to stay productive as work and the economy change. Each workshop builds one: framing a problem, telling a story, working in a team, using digital and AI tools well.
items.more: That makes them a natural next step for digital opportunity programs: once someone's connected, a navigator can send them to us.

items.title: The open cycle
items.when: Every twelve weeks, join any time
items.body: A Build Cycle runs in the open, and anyone can join as a contributor at any time. In set windows, the community proposes problem situations and ways to tackle them. Teams of three to five form around the ones people want to build, and every cycle ends at a public Showcase.

items.title: Sector cohorts
items.body: Inside the open cycle, a cohort of people who applied takes on one sector's problem situations, with Mentors from that sector: health care, cybersecurity, public service, manufacturing, or whichever a sponsor chooses. What they make goes back into the open cycle, and on to every Lab.

better.title: Open to every contribution. Kept by what works.
better.lede: Anyone can add a workshop, a playbook, a tool or a proposal. There are no formal requirements. What we keep, share and build on is decided by how it performs: what people make with it, and what happens for them next. The best of every Lab rises and spreads to the others. What doesn't work stays where it is.

delivery.title: Delivery is earned.
delivery.body: We're introducing a common standard for the people who run our workshops and Pods: they train for the role, then earn it by doing it well, signed off by people who already have. So every Lab delivers the same method, whoever's in the room.

options.title: Five ways to work with us.

items.title: Sponsor a sector cohort
items.body: Bring the sector, its problem situations, and two or three employers or agency teams who own them. We recruit and run the cohort inside the next cycle, through to the Showcase. You keep the solutions and the playbooks, and you meet the people who made them.

items.title: Host a Lab
items.body: Your public libraries and community spaces provide the rooms, a staff liaison, and a line to your navigators and job centres. We bring the workshops, the open cycle, and the volunteers who run them.

items.title: Adopt the playbooks
items.body: Run our workshops and the Build Cycle in your own programs, free. We can train your staff to run them.

items.title: Refer people
items.body: Workforce boards, job centres, navigators and agencies can send people to workshops and cohorts, including workers whose jobs are changing or have ended.

items.title: Fund Mentors
items.body: Mentors turn every obstacle a team hits into a workshop for the next team. Stipends, service-year positions or loaned staff time keep them in the room.

started.title: Built by the people it was for.
started.body: In fall 2025, fifty former federal workers met at DC Public Library to work out their next move together. From that group came The Labs, so anyone could do the same.

procure.title: The details.
items: The Upskilling Labs is a fiscally sponsored project of Superbloom Design, a 501(c)(3).
A common standard for the people who deliver our programs is being introduced this year.
Taking part is free for residents. Using the playbooks is free, and needs no contract.
Code is MIT-licensed, and everything else is CC BY 4.0.
We partner on library, workforce and digital opportunity grants.
On request: a capability statement, a sample agreement, and our data and Mentor policies.
